title: Lazy gas, hot gas, and a thousand robots
abstract: Amazon Robotics operates over a million robots across more than 300 warehouses worldwide. Inside a single warehouse, thousands of robots share the floor, moving inventory for order fulfillment and stock replenishment. Finding efficient, collision-free robot paths to their destinations is therefore essential for smooth operations. Let us formulate the underlying multiagent pathfinding (MAPF) problem a bit more precisely. Consider a typical warehouse layout as a W x H rectangular grid. At each time step, a robot can make one of five choices: move north, east, west, or south, or wait. These choices must be coordinated to avoid collisions. Over a planning horizon of T time steps, finding optimal robot paths involves approximately n = 5WHT binary decision variables, giving 2n possible combinations before accounting for feasibility constraints. Finding optimal paths that minimize the total move cost or arrival time without collisions is NP hard in general and can become computationally intractable even for moderate numbers of robots. In a paper we presented at this year’s International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), we show that physics offers a way around this intractability: plan trajectories as if the robots were particles of gas. Modeling the robots as a cold, lazy gas, whose particles spend only the minimum effort to reach their destinations, yields optimal, minimum-energy paths. This is equivalent to treating trajectory planning as an optimal-transport problem. It yields optimal paths, but computing them may take too long for real-time deployment. Modeling the fleet as a hot gas, whose particles jitter randomly along the way, yields trajectories that are computationally faster but potentially suboptimal. As the temperature drops to zero, however, the jittery hot-gas paths settle onto the lazy-gas ones. Our approach uses a Schrödinger bridge — a hot-gas model — to efficiently approximate the solution to an optimal-transport problem — the cold-gas model. Optimal transport To develop the formal connection, let us travel back to 1781 in France to meet Gaspard Monge, the father of differential geometry. Monge was looking for the most efficient way to transport excavated dirt to military fortifications. His studies gave rise to the optimal-transport problem, which asks how to transport resources from a set of sources to a set of destinations while minimizing cost, such as distance traveled or work done. Monge’s sources were the locations containing dirt. His formulation required all mass at each source location to be transported to one destination, producing a deterministic transport map. Although intuitive, Monge’s original formulation is a difficult nonlinear optimization problem with a potential combinatorial explosion in discrete settings. Finding an optimal map is therefore technically challenging and, in some settings, impossible. Roughly 150 years later, Soviet mathematician Leonid Kantorovich relaxed this restriction by allowing mass from one source to be split among multiple destinations. His key insight was that this relaxation converts a difficult optimization over transport maps into a linear program, a class of problems for which highly efficient computer algorithms were subsequently developed. Kantorovich received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to the theory of optimum allocation of resources. Optimal transport connects two mass distributions, also known as marginals, through minimum-cost transport plans. This two-marginal formulation represents only the initial and final configurations and the cost of transporting between them, not the intermediate paths or collisions along those paths. Formulating MAPF as optimal transport therefore requires a multistage approach, because robots generally cannot move from their starting locations to their destinations in a single time step; their locations must also be represented at every intermediate time. abstract: Today we are announcing the general availability of the trusted access program API on Amazon Bedrock . The API gives you one place to discover, request, and enroll in model provider trusted access programs. We are also announcing the public preview of the first two offerings for Claude models: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) and Enterprise Data Controls (EDC). Both are available on Amazon Bedrock, including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP). Frontier AI labs require stricter safety monitoring policies to their most capable models, and those policies still apply on Amazon Bedrock. For eligible customers, model providers also offer customers more control on how those policies are met, such as where retained data is stored and how it is reviewed. Each offering has its own terms, approvals, and settings. The Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API gives every provider offering one consistent Amazon Bedrock experience. Your teams discover offerings, check eligibility, and enroll in the same way for every provider. Your administrators decide who can enroll, using existing IAM policies and service control policies. As more model providers add offerings, those appear in the same place. EFS and EDC were built in partnership between AWS and Anthropic. They let you access Anthropic’s most capable models safely, from both a model use and a customer data perspective. With both EFS and EDC, when automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for your team to review. With EFS, customers store their data in their own AWS account, and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic or Amazon Bedrock. With EDC, retained data is stored in Amazon-managed storage instead of your account and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic. One application gives access to both offerings. In this post, we explain how the trusted access program API works, then walk through EFS and EDC storage options and setup. How trusted access programs work A trusted access program is a named provider program that gives customers more control of safety reviews and access to model capabilities in exchange for accepting the program’s terms. Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API now gives you one place to find the model and use case programs available to your account. EFS and EDC are the first offerings available today. Offerings that providers add later appear in the same place and follow the same steps. The status tells you what to do next. eligible means you’re eligible for the offering and can enroll, requestable means you need approval for eligibility first, and the statusReason field in the response explains how to request it. The model provider (or AWS, as authorized by the model provider) approves your eligibility. Enrolling is a separate step where you accept the offering’s terms imposed by the provider. You enroll at the scope where you were approved: an account, every account in an organization from the management account, or a single project. You can opt out at any time. Each step is a call to the trusted access program API, so you control who can enroll with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and service control policies (SCPs). More information is available in the trusted access programs documentation . Assessing AI Impact: Notes for Your CFO
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Hi there. This is the epilogue to my series on assessing the impact of AI-assisted software development. It brings all the concepts together into one whole. It’s also good for sharing with your CFO and other members of your leadership team. You can find the beginning of the series here: Are You Getting Your Money’s Worth from AI? The rest of the articles are linked below. Comfy? Great. Let’s get started. Give me the shortest possible version AI-assisted software development is expensive, and while the potential returns are high, they’re not yet proven. The field is changing rapidly, so learning the right approach requires experimentation and measurement. Spending varies by an order of magnitude: from hundreds of dollars per person per month to thousands. To know which approach is best, you need to measure impact as well as costs. The fullest view involves modeling the ROI of your software initiatives, which requires leadership support and cross-departmental participation. For a faster and more targeted view, ask your engineering leaders to measure changes in software development speed. But don’t just look at what you’re getting now; consider the long-term effects of unintended consequences and the possibility of lock-in. Say more about AI program fundamentals Measuring the costs of an AI-assisted software development program is fairly easy, but measuring benefits is harder. It’s tempting to use easy, shallow approaches that don’t consider the full picture. Some token costs are heavily subsidized, so prices could go up. Examples include subscriptions with generous token allowances and temporary promotions. On the other hand, competition could drive prices down. As you forecast ROI, consider optimistic and pessimistic cost scenarios. Consider that the fastest approaches might not be the most cost-effective. The best investment might involve lower per-person delivery speed, but much lower token costs, especially if the money for AI comes at the cost of headcount. Read more about why you should measure impact, and what you shouldn’t measure, in part 1 . What was that about modeling ROI? Most organizations primarily think in terms of cost and predictability, with minimal attention to value. Modeling ROI will not only help you understand AI’s impact, it will give you a better understanding of your software development efforts in general. Product development can create a model that calculates an initiative’s net present value. This requires cross-departmental participation, backing from Leadership and Finance, and some educated guesses. It will never reflect real value perfectly—it involves too many guesses and assumptions—but it makes those assumptions concrete and focuses people on what you’re getting for your money. Read more about modeling software’s business impact in part 4 . I just want to know if AI is faster Engineering leaders can get a narrower read on AI’s impact by measuring how it changes software delivery speed. They can also compare one approach to another, which will allow them to find the optimal blend of speed and costs for your company. Simplistic speed measurements abound. When evaluating claims, look for evidence of sophistication, such as randomized comparisons, and look for sustained results across numerous teams. Beware of measurements that simply count deliverables or changes in “velocity.” They’re not standardized. The pressure to demonstrate results from AI is immense, and the stories of success that are shared in conferences and executive circles grow with each retelling. Calibrate your skepticism accordingly. Listen for how the storytellers measured impact. Look for evidence of sustained results, not cherry-picked examples. title: Trusting an Agent Beyond Your Expertise
abstract: I have a Raspberry Pi on my home network running Pi-hole, a flight tracking setup, and a few services around them, with an external solid-state drive attached to it. When I first described the machine to my coding agent, I said there was nothing particularly complicated or compute intensive running on it, or so I thought. Every so often, the Pi would stop responding, and a reboot was the only way I could bring it back. Eventually it became annoying enough that I really wanted to find out what had happened. The logs I needed seemed to disappear with the restart, so I had a way to recover the machine and very little idea of how to investigate the failure. My Linux knowledge covers the things I’ve needed for server-side Java development over the years, and I can find my way around a terminal or follow familiar procedures. System-wide container configuration, service dependencies, and the details of IPv4 and IPv6 take me well beyond that experience. I knew enough to recognize that changing some of those settings could cut off my access and leave me running up the stairs to wire my computer up to the Pi. My dad also depends on this machine for his flight radar app and enjoys watching planes go by, so I had to consider how a change would affect him too. Before I could consider changing any of those settings, I needed help deciding where to look. Somebody had to turn “The Pi has stopped responding” into questions I could investigate, and I decided that asking the agent was a reasonable way to do that. It went a little too well, to be honest. The agent configured persistent logging and regular health samples so there would be information to examine after a restart. We moved to Ethernet and disabled Wi-Fi, and it checked the services, storage, and connection to the router. It later repaired forwarding for local name queries and identified a problem in the order in which the Pi-hole container stopped and its external drive was unmounted. The container needed the drive to stay mounted until the service had stopped, so the agent added an explicit dependency on the drive’s mount to put those events in the right order. After I later installed updates and rebooted, I asked it to check again, and it found log entries showing the service stopping, followed by a successful unmount of the drive. I could follow those steps once the agent explained them to me: finding the missing dependency, expressing it in the service configuration, and choosing the log entries to examine all required knowledge I was getting from the agent. I trusted its assessment of that reboot, relying on it to judge changes it had made with the root access I had given it over SSH. That felt very weird and gave me reason to think more carefully about the advice to “trust, but verify.” Checking a repair I needed help to make The agent also suggested the configuration backups and checks after changes, so I relied on it for the precautions as well as the repair. Judging whether I could recover from a failed change required some of the same Linux knowledge I just didn’t have. In “ Code Review After Code Gets Cheap ,” I described starting with intended behavior, evidence, and the effects of a change elsewhere in the system. Adjusting enough of the specification to make correctness checkable also depends on knowing what to expect. With my Pi challenges, I needed help establishing those expectations while deciding whether to accept the change, which left me wondering how likely this approach was to succeed and how much trust was justified. I had given my agent the ability to act on the assessment I was asking it to make. With root access over SSH, it could change the operating system and services, including settings that determined whether I could reach the machine again. My willingness to let it proceed depended partly on what I thought a mistake would cost me. title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
abstract: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand. Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently. The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars , who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off . The arm was developed in the 2000s , initially trialed in 2014 , and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying. Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system. The loss of a limb In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground. The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated. Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.” Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says. The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says. New connections A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab . Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
abstract: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right. Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence. Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here? If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today. But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants. If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue. PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand. This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there. And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation. This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead. It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source. But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
abstract: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy. Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.” Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget. As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent. Transparency, monetized The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town. This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc .” Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says. SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
abstract: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. title: Why Does Voice AI Still Struggle With Kenyans’ Speech?
abstract: When people read prepared text aloud, AI can transcribe Swahili with remarkably few errors, and Swahili speech recognition looks close to solved. A March 2026 preprint by a team including a Harvard University researcher reports a 3.24 percent word-error rate on recordings from Mozilla’s Common Voice collection of volunteer-recorded speech. But Kenyans rarely talk like Common Voice volunteers. They switch between Swahili and English mid-sentence, drop in Sheng slang that changes by neighborhood, speak with accents shaped by their first languages, and contend with public-transport noise on low-end handsets. Another 2026 preprint , which covers 20 African languages, argues that this kind of spontaneous, noisy, overlapping audio exposes a generalization gap that scaling laws built on the English language have not closed. Voice has become a main interface for many Kenyans, as WhatsApp voice notes and chatbot voice prompts gain popularity in a country that ranks first globally on AI usage. But if an AI model cannot parse everyday speech, it quietly excludes the people it was meant to serve. “My iPhone’s Siri is unable to follow my voice command in Sheng or Swahili,” says Loise Lionah, a beautician in Nairobi. “ChatGPT tries to understand but gets the meaning wrong. The case is similar with Gemini and Claude.” Swahili Dialects and Sheng Challenge Voice AI Swahili, also called Kiswahili, is one of Kenya’s two official languages, alongside English. A Bantu language of the East African coast, Swahili is spoken by more than 200 million people across 14 African countries. Tanzania is regarded as the home of standard Swahili. Yet Catherine Mangare , an AI and computing lecturer at Tanzania’s Sokoine University of Agriculture and a Ph.D. candidate at Okayama University in Japan, says even there, the standard is only the baseline. “Standard Kiswahili is a useful starting point,” she says, “but Tanzanian speech varies by region and setting.” Sheng, spoken and understood by about 60 percent of Kenyans, adds another layer. This Swahili variant, which emerged among Nairobi’s urban youth many decades ago, follows Swahili grammar but borrows from English, Kenyan mother tongues, and even Hindi, Spanish, and American slang, and it has no standard spelling. Linguists label it a language in constant flux : For example, the Sheng word for “girl” fluctuates according to generation, location, and social media trends. “Sheng itself is highly broken down per region,” says Tehillah Kachila , founder and CEO of Nairobi-based Zabibu Technika, a startup that builds the Fikra family of Swahili AI models. Kachila says the most recent Sheng dataset dates back to 2019—a major reason, he argues, why prominent voice AI systems struggle to respond accurately to Sheng prompts. Lilian Wanzare, shown leading a voice-data collection workshop, develops speech datasets for Kenyan languages to help AI systems understand a wider range of speakers. Maseno Centre for Applied AI Building Speech Datasets for African Languages The supply of recorded Swahili speech is growing. The African Next Voices project , supported by a US $2.2 million Gates Foundation grant, has recorded 9,000 hours across 18 languages. Lilian Wanzare , who leads the project’s Kenyan component at Maseno University’s Centre for Applied AI, puts its Kenyan output at roughly 3,000 hours of transcribed speech. title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
abstract: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it. A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note. Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO 2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO 2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO 2 . That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane. Read full article Comments

title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
abstract: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory. Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation. But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next. Read full article Comments

abstract: Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze's privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers. Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.” The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers. title: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites
abstract: In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers. If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold. "The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth." Read full article Comments

title: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
abstract: Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault . After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it's an installable package with automatic updating. Ladybird is most notable for what it isn't: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google's Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird's rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. "The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork," project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday's announcement. "The browser around it is modest, but functional." title: Etsy clarifies AI terms after seller backlash
abstract: After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the company to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance. In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the company's terms of service and admitted that her team "should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content." “Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we're using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.” Read full article Comments

title: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop
abstract: Drone attacks on data centers. Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion. In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine: We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there's an incentive to target it. Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers: Read full article Comments

title: Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets
abstract: On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran. Although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China . In a press release , however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security. The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. title: Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl
abstract: In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound. The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate. Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast. Read full article Comments

title: A familiar Iranian hacking group has found a new way to cause chaos
abstract: One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history : cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food. Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command. title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
abstract: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics. LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online. The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI. Read full article Comments

title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
abstract: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks. The missions affected by the outages — hopefully temporary — are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history. Losing its voice The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate. Read full article Comments

title: Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
abstract: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters , Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide. Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote. The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report , dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident. title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
abstract: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset. It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math. Tackling Riemann The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field." Read full article Comments

title: Back-to-back measles deaths is our new reality; US tally now at 14
abstract: Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water. The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23 . Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died. Deaths and transmission On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death , an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child . New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby . On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4 . Read full article Comments

title: Amazon drone crashes on garage after delivering shampoo, draws FAA probe
abstract: An Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States. The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit . After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines. “Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7. title: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can
abstract: A European Ariane 6 launcher propelled 36 satellites into orbit for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation Tuesday, continuing the network's build-out after 40 satellites were lost earlier this month during a failure of United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket . The launch was an important rebound for Amazon, bringing the Amazon Leo fleet to 432 satellites as the company seeks to fill the void left by the grounding of ULA's Vulcan rocket, Amazon's primary launch provider. Now, an Amazon official tells Ars it is accelerating several Falcon 9 launches the company has purchased from SpaceX, which also owns the Starlink satellite network that Amazon seeks to dethrone. The next Falcon 9 launch for Amazon Leo is now planned for December, Amazon said, moved forward from its previous launch date next year. Several more Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites in rapid succession after the December flight. Read full article Comments

title: Jetpack Compose 기반 커스텀 3D 캐러셀 개발기
abstract: Jetpack Compose(안드로이드의 선언형 UI 툴킷)로 가로로 넘기는 목록을 만들 때는 대부분 LazyRow 부터 떠올리실 겁니다. 그런데 최근 저희 팀에서 만든 화면 중에는 아무리 고민해도 LazyRow 로는 만들 수 없는 UI가 있었습니다. 이 글에서는 그 UI를 커스텀 3D 캐러셀로 직접 만든 경험을 소개하고, 그 과정에서 만난 다음 세 가지 이슈를 어떻게 풀었는지 정리합니다. 드래그하는 동안 매 프레임 바뀌는 값을 '리컴포지션'(상태가 바뀌어 컴포저블 함수가 다시 실행되는 것) 없이 카드 여러 장에 전달하기 y축으로 기울인 카드를 눌렀더니 엉뚱한 카드가 열리는 '3D 터치 판정 버그'(Compose 1.7.0부터) LazyRow 없이 'Paging 3'로 다음 페이지를 불러오기 마지막으로 이 UI를 AI와 함께 만들며 배운 점도 덧붙입니다. ThingsBook과 두 가지 UI ThingsBook은 네이버가 북미를 대상으로 출시한 SNS 서비스입니다. 책이나 영화, 음악 같은 여러 취미를 글감으로 골라 기록을 남기고, 피드에서 다른 사람의 기록을 둘러보고, 내가 쌓은 기록을 카테고리별로 묶어 나만의 책장에 꽂아 둘 수 있습니다. 문제의 UI는 세 번째 화면인 '모아보기'에 있습니다. 모아보기에는 아이템을 나열하는 방식이 두 가지 있습니다. 왼쪽은 책장형 UI, 오른쪽은 카드형 UI입니다. 책장형 UI : 책장에 책이 꽂혀 있듯이 책등이 늘어서 있고, 손가락으로 넘기면 선택된 책이 3D로 펼쳐지면서 표지가 나타납니다. 카드형 UI : 카드들이 비스듬히 기울어진 채 겹겹이 쌓여 있습니다. 넘기면 맨 앞 카드는 눕듯이 빠지고, 다음 카드가 일어서면서 앞으로 나옵니다. 이 둘 중 하나는 LazyRow 로 만들 수 있었고, 하나는 그렇지 않았습니다. LazyRow 로 만들 수 없는 것은 어느 쪽이었을까요? 정답은 이 글에서 만든 3D 캐러셀인 '카드형 UI'입니다. 책이 3D로 펼쳐지는 책장형 UI가 훨씬 복잡해 보이지만, 책장형 UI는 LazyRow 위에서 동작합니다. 반대로 겉보기에는 카드 몇 장이 겹쳐 있을 뿐인 카드형 UI는 LazyRow 를 쓸 수 없었습니다. 왜 LazyRow로는 안 되는가 먼저 LazyRow 가 무엇을 약속하는지 짚고, 카드형 UI가 그 약속과 어디서 어긋나는지 차례로 살펴보겠습니다. LazyRow가 약속하는 세 가지 LazyRow 를 쓴다는 것은 사실 LazyRow 와 세 가지 약속을 하는 것입니다. 배치 : 아이템은 겹치지 않고 한 줄로 섭니다. 그래서 어떤 아이템의 위치는 앞 아이템들의 폭에 일정한 간격( spacedBy )을 더한 값이 됩니다. 스크롤 : 손가락을 1픽셀 움직이면 모든 아이템이 똑같이 1픽셀씩 움직입니다. 목록 전체가 한 덩어리로 평행이동합니다. 보이는 것만 컴포즈 : 화면에 보이는 아이템만 컴포즈(컴포저블 함수를 실행해 UI를 만드는 일)하고, 화면 밖 아이템은 아예 만들지 않습니다. 그래서 이름에 'Lazy'가 붙었고, 긴 목록에서도 효율적으로 동작합니다. 이 세 가지를 기억해 두고 카드형 UI를 살펴보겠습니다. 카드형 UI에 숨은 네 종류의 카드 카드형 UI를 구성 요소별로 나누어 보면, 카드의 종류가 네 가지나 있습니다. 포커스 카드 : 지금 선택된 카드입니다. 정면(0°)을 보고 있고 크기는 100%입니다. 다음 카드 : 포커스 카드 뒤에 넓은 간격(90dp)을 두고, 45° 기울어진 채 다음 차례를 기다립니다. 뒤 카드들 : 훨씬 좁은 간격(30dp)으로 겹겹이 쌓여 있습니다. 모두 똑같이 기울어져 있고, 크기는 85%입니다. 지나간 카드 : 넘겨서 지나간 카드는 왼쪽에 조각처럼 남아, 앞에 어떤 카드가 있었는지를 살짝 보여 줍니다. 이 글의 수치(간격 90dp·30dp, 한 장 넘기는 거리 200dp 등)는 설명을 위해 실제 앱 값에서 단순하게 바꾼 값입니다. dp는 화면 밀도와 관계없이 쓰는 안드로이드의 길이 단위입니다. 이 구조를 LazyRow 의 세 가지 약속에 하나씩 대어 보겠습니다. 약속 ① 배치: 간격이 카드마다 다르고, 넘기는 동안 바뀐다 LazyRow 의 간격은 spacedBy 로 정하는 값 하나이고, 모든 아이템 사이에 똑같이 들어갑니다. 반면 카드형 UI는 포커스 카드와 바로 다음 카드 사이의 간격만 90dp로, 다른 카드들 사이의 간격인 30dp보다 훨씬 넓습니다. 넘기기 전에는 0번과 1번 카드 사이가 90dp이고, 한 장 넘긴 뒤에는 1번과 2번 카드 사이가 90dp가 됩니다. 더 곤란한 점은, 넘기는 동안 이 넓은 간격이 다음 쌍으로 옮겨 간다는 것입니다. 30dp였던 간격이 90dp로 벌어지고, 90dp였던 간격은 지나간 카드와 함께 멀어집니다. 간격 자체가 애니메이션이므로 spacedBy 하나로는 표현할 수 없습니다. 약속 ② 스크롤: 같은 드래그에 카드마다 움직이는 거리가 다르다 LazyRow 에서는 손가락이 움직인 만큼 모든 아이템이 똑같이 움직여야 합니다. 카드형 UI에서 카드 한 장을 넘기려면 손가락을 200dp 정도 끌어야 한다고 해 보겠습니다. 포커스 카드는 손가락을 거의 그대로 따라가서, 왼쪽으로 200dp 이동하면서 45° 눕습니다. 다음 카드는 200dp가 아닌 90dp만 이동하고, 기울어지는 방향도 반대입니다. 45°에서 0°로 일어섭니다. 뒤 카드들은 30dp만 움직이고, 기울기는 아예 변하지 않습니다. LazyRow 였다면 모든 카드가 손가락과 똑같이 200dp를 움직여야 합니다. 카드형 UI의 스크롤은 단순한 평행이동이 아니라, 카드마다 다른 규칙으로 움직여야 합니다. 약속 ③ 보이는 것만 컴포즈: 한 화면에 카드 8장이 겹쳐 보인다 다음 그림에서 점선으로 표시한 범위가 사용자 기기의 화면 폭(360dp)이라고 해 보겠습니다. 카드가 좁은 간격으로 겹쳐 있다 보니, 이 화면 안에 8장이 동시에 보입니다. 보이는 것만 만들어서 비용을 아낀다는 LazyRow 의 장점이 크게 줄어들 수밖에 없습니다. 게다가 LazyRow 는 각 아이템이 보이는지를 '레이아웃상의 자리'로 판단합니다. 카드형 UI를 흉내 내려면 LazyRow 가 정해 준 자리에서 카드를 graphicsLayer 로 옮겨 그려야 하는데, 그러면 LazyRow 가 '화면 밖'이라고 판단해 만들지 않은 카드가 실제로는 화면 안에 그려져야 하는 상황이 생깁니다. 판단과 화면이 어긋나는 것입니다. 결론: LazyRow를 쓸 수 없었다 세 가지 약속과 카드형 UI를 나란히 놓아 보면 다음과 같습니다. 약속 카드형 UI ① 배치 간격이 카드마다 다르고, 넘기는 동안 넓은 간격이 다음 쌍으로 옮겨 간다. ② 스크롤 같은 드래그에 포커스 카드는 200dp, 다음 카드는 90dp, 뒤 카드들은 30dp를 움직인다. 평행이동이 아니다. ③ 보이는 것만 컴포즈 한 화면에 8장이 겹쳐 보이고, 옮겨 그리면 '보이는지' 판단도 화면과 어긋난다. 세 가지 약속을 전부 어기게 되므로 카드형 UI에는 LazyRow 를 쓸 수 없었습니다. 카드형 UI의 동작 원리 그렇다면 LazyRow 없이 카드형 UI를 어떻게 만들었는지 살펴보겠습니다. 상태는 Float 하나, ratio 카드형 UI의 모든 상태는 Float 변수 하나에 들어 있습니다. @Stable class PortraitCarouselState { // 몇 번째 카드인가(연속값) var ratio by mutableFloatStateOf( 0f ) } val carouselState = remember { PortraitCarouselState () } 핵심은 ratio 라는 값 하나입니다. 지금 몇 번째 카드가 보이고 있는지를 연속값으로 담습니다. 예를 들어 ratio 가 2.0이면 2번 카드가 정면에 와 있는 상태이고, 2.3이면 2번 카드에서 3번 카드로 30% 넘어가는 중이라는 뜻입니다. 즉, 이 값은 LazyRow 처럼 픽셀 단위의 스크롤 오프셋이 아니라 '카드 단위의 위치'입니다. LazyRow 는 픽셀 오프셋을 들고 있지만, 카드형 UI는 '몇 번째 카드인가'를 들고 있습니다. 드래그한 '픽셀'을 카드 '개수'로 환산 이제 손가락 동작을 ratio 로 바꿔야 합니다. LazyRow 대신 카드 영역 전체를 감

title: 운영자의 시간을 아끼는 AI 에이전트 2부 - MCP 부터 Agent 설계까지
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 발표 내용 운영 문의가 들어오면 운영자는 로그와 메트릭, 과거 사례를 직접 살펴보고 답변해야 합니다. 업무 시간 밖에 들어온 문의는 첫 답변을 받기까지 약 13시간이 걸리기도 했습니다. 이 발표에서는 OpenSearch 운영 문의에 운영자보다 먼저 답변하는 AI 에이전트, care-ai를 만들면서 겪은 시행착오를 소개합니다. 그 과정에서 얻은 설계 원칙과 개선 효과를 실제 사례와 수치로 공유합니다. ​ <참고> 운영자의 시간을 아끼는 AI 에이전트 1부 - RCA·Q&A 운영 지식 그래프 ​ 발표 대상 LLM 에이전트를 운영 업무에 적용하려는 분 MCP 서버와 도구를 설계하는 분 에이전트 답변의 정확도와 신뢰성을 높이고 싶은 분 ​ 목차 Episode 1. 처음 만든 에이전트 필요한 정보가 모두 있었는데도, 에이전트는 왜 원인을 확정하지 못했을까요? Episode 2. MCP 응답 설계 도구 응답 하나가 모델의 입력 한도를 넘었습니다. 이 문제를 계기로 모델에는 요약을 먼저 제공하고, 원본 데이터는 요청할 때만 반환하도록 MCP 서버를 바꿨습니다. 24회 평가에서 정답은 10회에서 17회로 늘었고, 토큰 사용량은 26% 줄었습니다. Episode 3. 모델 vs 코드 모델의 판단에 맡길 일과 코드로 결정할 일은 어떻게 나눠야 할까요? 모델은 탐색과 판단을, 코드는 근거 검증과 최종 판정을 맡도록 구조를 바꿨습니다. 그 결과, 같은 문의를 세 번 평가했을 때 정확한 원인을 답한 횟수가 0회에서 3회로 늘었습니다. Episode 4. 답변 설계 운영자는 무엇을 어떤 순서로 설명할까요? 운영자의 답변 방식을 참고해 상태, 확인한 값, 원인, 다음 조치와 담당자를 정해진 순서로 전달하도록 했습니다. 요청자에게 보낼 답변과 운영자가 확인할 카드도 분리했습니다. Episode 5. 결과 첫 응답 시간의 중앙값은 47초였습니다. 운영자 댓글 수는 38% 줄었고, 문의가 종료되기까지 걸리는 시간은 절반으로 줄었습니다. 운영자가 직접 답변한 문의의 비율도 약 95%에서 60%로 낮아졌습니다. 데모: 주문 데이터 문의부터 답변까지 테스트 클러스터에 미리 준비한 사례로, 주문 데이터에 관한 문의를 접수한 care-ai가 답변을 내놓기까지의 과정을 보여드립니다. ​ ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: OmniEvaluator: AI 모델과 에이전트를 위한 통합 평가 프레임워크
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 발표 내용 AI 서비스를 만들 때 "이 모델, 우리 서비스에 써도 될까?"라는 질문은 도입 전(후보 모델·API·툴 조합 비교)과 도입 후(의도대로 서빙되는지, 패치·버전별 차이) 반복해서 돌아옵니다. 그런데 이 질문에 답하는 비용은 큽니다. 모달리티마다 평가 툴킷이 다르고, 같은 벤치마크라도 프롬프트·파서·메트릭 구현에 따라 점수가 수십 점씩 갈라지며, 결과는 사람 손으로 모아야 합니다. ​ OmniEvaluator는 이 문제를 구조적으로 푸는 통합 평가 프레임워크입니다. 추론 엔진 4종(HF Transformers·vLLM·SGLang·상용 API)과 평가 프레임워크 4종(lm-eval-harness·lmms-eval·VLMEvalKit·built-in)을 하나의 중간 스키마로 연결해 텍스트·이미지·비디오·오디오 1,000개 이상의 벤치마크를 하나의 인터페이스로 실행합니다. 모든 실행은 설정·예측·점수를 담은 아티팩트로 남아 그대로 재현할 수 있고, CPU에서 도는 내장 Verifier가 프롬프트·프레임워크 차이에 흔들리지 않는 채점 신호를 제공합니다. 2026년에는 Agent Harness가 추가되어 기존 벤치마크에 옵션 두 개만 붙이면 툴 호출 궤적까지 채점하는 Agent 평가로 전환되며, 대시보드에서 요청 → 진행 → 결과 → 샘플을 한곳에서 확인할 수 있습니다. ​ 관련 자료 논문: A Composable Evaluation System for Reproducible Omni-Modal Foundation Model Evaluation (EMNLP 2026 System Demonstrations, arXiv 2609.01315) 공개 저장소 : https://github.com/naver-ai/omni-evaluator ​ 발표 대상 AI 서비스 기획자: 서비스 도입 전 후보 모델·API·툴 조합의 구현 가능성과 가치를 정량적으로 비교하려는 분 AI Engineer / Forward Deployment Engineer: 도입 후 모델이 의도대로 서빙되는지, 패치·버전·서빙엔진별 차이를 정량 확인하려는 분 모델 평가 담당자: 여러 모달리티·프레임워크에 걸친 평가 환경을 하나로 통합하려는 분 ​ 목차 평가의 어려움 OmniEvaluator 구조 Agent Harness 대시보드 — 리더보드, 샘플 뷰어, Trigger Claude Plugin 팀 운영 사례 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: 디자인 시스템이 있는데도 화면은 왜 제각각일까?
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스뱅크에서 대출 심사 플랫폼을 디자인하는 Product Designer 신재희입니다. 대출 심사 플랫폼은 대출 신청 건을 검토하고 처리하는 내부 업무 툴이에요. 이 툴은 대출 상품마다 화면이 제각각이었고, 저는 이걸 하나의 구조로 묶는 일을 맡게 되었는데요. 오늘은 복잡한 업무 툴에 일관성을 만들기 위해 무엇을 이해하고, 어떻게 기준을 세웠는지를 이야기해 보려고 해요. 같은 업무인데, 화면은 제각각인 툴 대출 심사 플랫폼은 대출 운영 담당자가 매일 사용하는 업무 툴이에요. 담당자들은 이곳에서 대출 신청 건을 열어 정보와 서류에 문제가 없는지, 다음 단계로 넘어가도 되는지를 확인하죠. 팀에 처음 합류해 제품을 써 봤을 때 가장 먼저 느낀 건 일관성이 없다는 거였어요. 신용대출, 주택담보대출 등 대출 상품별로 처리 흐름이 다른 건 자연스러운 일이지만, 같은 목적의 행동까지 상품마다 다른 방식으로 만들어져 있었다는 게 문제 였어요. 예를 들어 대출 심사는 크게 신청자 정보 확인, 서류 검토, 각 단계의 결과 확정 순서 로 진행돼요. 이때 확정 은 심사 과정에서 중요한 행동이에요. 그런데 이 버튼이 주택담보대출에서는 화면 하단의 가장 우측, 전세자금대출에서는 좌측 안에 놓여 있었어요 . 단계마다 주요 과업 버튼이 노출되는 방식도 상품별로 제각각이었고요. 운영 담당자가 주택담보대출을 담당하다가 전세대출팀으로 옮기면, 같은 업무를 하더라도 버튼의 위치와 사용 방식부터 다시 익혀야 했죠. 새로운 화면에 적응하고 교육하는 데 시간과 비용이 들었고, 그 부담은 고스란히 팀에 돌아갔어요. 디자인 시스템이 없던 것도 아니었어요. 버튼, 테이블, 필드 같은 기초 컴포넌트는 이미 있었죠. 그런데도 왜 이런 문제가 생겼을까요? 원인을 찾으려면 먼저 이 제품이 실제로 어떻게 쓰이고 있는지부터 이해해야 했어요. 고치기 전에, 먼저 이해하기 대출은 업무의 히스토리가 길고, 실수 하나가 큰 영향을 미치는 도메인이에요. 팀에 합류한 뒤 제품과 업무를 정확히 이해하기 위해 두 가지 방향으로 접근했어요. 1. 제품의 구조 분해하기 먼저 제품에서 수행해야 할 작업을 체크리스트로 만들었어요. 실제 개발 환경에서 체크리스트를 따라 과업을 하나씩 수행하며 제품을 파악해 보려 했죠. 그런데 같은 작업도 상품마다 화면 구성과 처리 방식이 달랐어요. 정해진 순서대로 체크리스트를 따라가는 것만으로는 각 상품의 흐름을 파악하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 서로 다른 대출 상품의 화면을 단계별로 캡처해 하나의 아트보드에 나란히 놓았어요. 세로에는 상품을, 가로에는 단계를 배치해 같은 단계끼리 비교했어요. 그러자 상품마다 다른 부분이 한눈에 보였어요. 예를 들어 같은 확인 단계인데도 어떤 상품은 모달로, 어떤 상품은 화면 안에서 바로 처리하고 있었어요. 이 차이를 PO와 엔지니어분들께 하나씩 여쭤봤어요. 업무상 필요해서 생긴 차이도 있었지만, 단순히 제품이 만들어진 시점이 달라서 생긴 차이도 있었어요. 이렇게 차이의 이유를 구분해 정리한 표가 이후 공통 패턴을 파악하는 출발점이 됐어요. 2. 사용자에게 직접 묻기 제품을 직접 써 보는 것만으로는 실제 업무 방식까지 파악하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 UX Researcher분의 도움을 받아 실제 운영 담당자분들을 인터뷰하며 일하는 모습을 가까이서 지켜봤어요. 그런데 제가 생각했던 업무 흐름과 실제로 일하는 방식이 크게 다르더라고요. 심사에는 단계가 있으니 업무도 순서대로 진행될 거라고 생각했어요. 정보를 확인하고, 다음 단계로 넘어가 서류를 보고, 마지막에 확정하는 식으로요. 그런데 실제 담당자분들은 앞 단계로 돌아가 다시 확인하기도 하고, 모니터 양쪽에 여러 화면을 띄워 둔 채 정보를 교차 검증하며 일하고 있었어요. 단계는 나뉘어 있었지만, 실제 업무가 그 순서대로만 진행되는 건 아니었죠. 이런 업무 방식을 관찰하면서 설계 방향도 달라졌어요. 순서대로 진행하는 흐름은 기본 패턴으로 두되, 교차 검증이 필요한 화면은 단계와 상관없이 언제든 조회할 수 있어야 했어요. 그래서 특정 화면을 새 창으로 띄우는 버튼처럼, 필요한 정보에 바로 접근할 수 있는 장치가 필요하다는 생각도 할 수 있었죠. 제품을 직접 써 보는 것만으로는 발견하기 어려웠던 요구사 항이었어요. 인터뷰를 통해 알게 된 내용 팁: 인터뷰는 도메인을 익힌 다음에 고맥락 제품이라면 너무 이른 시점의 인터뷰는 추천하지 않아요. 쓰는 용어도, 일하는 방식도 일상에서 접하는 도메인과 많이 다르거든요. 인터뷰어가 도메인을 얼마나 이해하고 있느냐에 따라 들을 수 있는 이야기의 깊이가 달라져요. 컴포넌트는 있었지만 기준은 없었다 제품을 이해하고 나니, 무엇을 통일하고 무엇을 상품별로 다르게 가져가야 할지가 보였어요. 모든 상품의 화면을 똑같이 만드는 게 아니라, 여러 상품에서 반복되는 화면과 행동에 일관된 기준을 세우는 게 중요했어요. 그동안 이 툴은 전담 디자이너 없이 각 팀의 요청에 맞춰 빠르게 확장되어 왔어요. 기존 디자인 시스템의 컴포넌트를 활용하되, 화면을 어떻게 구성하고 배치할지는 각 팀이 상황에 맞게 판단해야 했었죠. 빠른 대응이 우선이다 보니 공통된 기준을 세우기보다는 각자 필요한 방식으로 조합해 사용하는 일이 많았어요. 디자인 시스템은 있었지만, 이를 화면 단위로 어떻게 조합하고 배치할지에 대한 기준은 없었던 거예요. 그래서 컴포넌트를 더 만드는 대신, 여러 상품에서 반복되는 화면과 흐름을 화면 단위의 패턴으로 정의하기로 했어요. 대출 심사 과정에서 공통적으로 필요한 화면을 살펴보고, 크게 세 가지 패턴으로 나눴어요. 리스트 화면: 심사할 신청 건을 찾고 선택하는 화면 단계별 작업 화면: 신청자 정보와 서류를 검토하는 화면 부가 정보 영역: 교차 검증에 필요한 정보를 언제든 확인할 수 있는 영역 정의한 패턴은 제품 안에서 패키지화해 어떤 상품을 작업하든 가져다 쓸 수 있도록 만들었어요. 확정 같은 핵심 행동의 위치와 동작 방식도 패턴에 포함했어요. 기존 컴포넌트만으로 표현하기 어려운 부분은 새로운 구조를 만들어 보완했고요. 이렇게 화면 단위의 패턴까지 갖추면서 디자인 시스템을 확장할 수 있었어요. 덕분에 새 상품을 작업할 때마다 화면 구조를 처음부터 고민할 필요가 없어졌어요. 이미 정의된 패턴을 바탕으로 상품에 필요한 구성을 선택하고 조합하는 것부터 설계를 시작할 수 있게 됐습니다. AI로 구축한 DLOS Docs 이렇게 합의한 패턴과 규칙은 문서로도 정리했어요. 이전에는 설계 결정이 업무 메신저와 여러 문서에 흩어져 있었어요. 누군가 물어볼 때마다 같은 설명을 반복해야 했고, 새 팀원이 오면 맥락을 처음부터 다시 공유해야 했어요. 그래서 AI를 활용해 패턴과 규칙을 한곳에서 확인할 수 있는 공통 문서를 만들게 됐어요. 이제 규칙에 대한 질문이 생기면 문서를 바탕으로 대화를 시작할 수 있게 됐어요. 만드는 것보다 어려웠던 것, 설득 좋은 패턴을 만들었다고 바로 쓰이진 않더라고요. 당시 상품들은 비즈니스적으로 빠르게 성장하고 있었고, 디자인 시스템을 적용하는 일은 당장의 우선순위가 아니었어요. 이미 각자의 방식으로 운영되던 팀들을 설득하는 과정은 생각보다 길고 어려웠어요. 공통 패턴을 사용해야 한다고 여러 번 공유해도, 어느새 다른 곳에서 새로운 패턴이 만들어져 있었어요. 그럴 때마다 해당 사례를 다시 팀으로 가져와 함께 살펴보고 기준을 맞춰야 했죠. 처음에는 공통 구조를 적용해야 한다는 점을 말로써 강조만 했어요. 하지만 몇 차례 커뮤니케이션을 거치면서 PO, PM분들이 실제로 걱정하는 게 무엇인지 알게 됐어요. 바로 속도였어요. 공통 구조를 적용하려면 기존 방식을 바꾸고 새로운 구조를 익혀야 하니, 당장의 출시가 늦어질 수 있다는 거였죠. 그때부터는 각 팀이 걱정하는 부분에 공감하면서 장기적으로 드는 비용까지 함께 생각해 보자고 이야기했어요. 각자 만들면 당장의 출시는 빠를 수 있지만, 상품이 늘어날 때마다 같은 구조를 다시 만들어야 하고 운영 담당자가 바뀔 때마다 새로운 화면을 익혀야 하니까요. 반대로 공통 구조가 쌓이면 다음 상품은 이미 정해진 패턴을 활용해 더 적은 시간과 노력으로 만들 수 있어요. 이런 이야기를 나누면서 공통 구조가 플랫폼팀만을 위한 기준이 아니

title: Why Can’t My Running Pods Be Reached? Our Journey to kube-proxy nftables Mode
abstract: Hi, I’m Karin, and I’m on the Cluster squad within SRE at Karrot. Our team designs and runs the Kubernetes platform that every service at Karrot runs on. We take responsibility for everything that keeps our clusters observable and reliable, from monitoring infrastructure all the way to the service mesh and security, along with the policies and roadmaps that keep it all maintainable. In this post, I’ll share how we migrated kube-proxy from iptables mode to nftables mode. kube-proxy runs on every node in a Kubernetes cluster and programs network rules into the Linux kernel so that traffic sent to a Service reaches the actual Pods. For years, our clusters ran kube-proxy in iptables mode to provide this core feature. Below, I’ll walk through how we moved to nftables, its more efficient successor, and what we learned along the way. 1. kube-proxy latency was hurting service reliability In Kubernetes, nodes come and go and Pods spin up all the time. That’s just how it works. But when a Pod lands on a fresh node and the app starts up, is it actually ready to talk to other services? kube-proxy manages the network rules (just “rules” from here on) on each node that let traffic headed for a Service reach the actual Pods . On a new node, if an application starts up while those rules are still being prepared, its DNS lookups and calls to other services can fail. kube-proxy rule sync lag had been creeping up for a while. We’d been watching the metrics since 2024, and latency was noticeably higher in our production cluster in the Korea region, the largest of all the regions we serve. But we judged it wasn’t serious enough to cause operational problems, and in practice, it never actually turned into an incident. Then, in the first half of this year, we made a big change: we adopted Karpenter. Now that we could scale out nodes quickly, we stopped using the Overprovisioner that used to keep spare nodes ready for Pods. As a result, Pods were landing on freshly created nodes much more often, which also raised the odds that an application would try to talk to something before rule sync had finished. Soon after, we started getting reports like the ones below, and most of them boiled down to “my Pod can’t talk to anything.” Putting our kube-proxy metrics from 2024 and 2026 side by side made it obvious how much heavier kube-proxy’s workload had gotten in just two years. Our service footprint and NAT rule count had grown noticeably, and Pods were being created and terminated far more often. Every time a Pod changes, the Service’s Endpoints (the IPs of the Pods that receive its traffic) change with it, so the number of changes kube-proxy had to apply grew right along with it. Rule sync latency got several times worse, and endpoint changes pending, which tracks Endpoint changes not yet reflected in the rules, went from occasional brief spikes to a steady backlog. With Endpoints constantly churning from deploys and autoscaling, and nodes repeatedly being torn down and spun up, the initial rule sync on a new node sometimes took as long as 4 minutes and 20 seconds . (That’s over four minutes with no working Service or DNS traffic!) Once we confirmed this was actually affecting production, we had to fix it. After some intense discussion with the team, we decided to try switching kube-proxy from iptables mode to nftables mode. Here’s how the two modes differ. In iptables mode, kube-proxy creates rules for every Service and every Endpoint. title: 파드는 떴는데 왜 통신이 안 될까? kube-proxy nftables 전환 여정
abstract: 안녕하세요, 당근 SRE팀 클러스터 파트에서 일하고 있는 Karin(카린)이에요. 클러스터 파트는 당근 내부의 모든 서비스가 운영되는 쿠버네티스 환경을 설계하고 관리해요. 쿠버네티스 환경의 가시성과 서비스 안정성을 확보하기 위해 모니터링 인프라부터 서비스 메시, 보안까지 여러 방면에서 정책과 로드맵을 설계하고 적용해요. 이 글에서는 kube-proxy를 iptables 모드에서 nftables 모드로 전환한 이야기를 해보려고 해요. kube-proxy는 쿠버네티스의 모든 노드에서 동작하면서, Service로 들어온 트래픽이 실제 Pod로 전달되도록 리눅스 커널에 네트워크 규칙을 설정하는 컴포넌트예요. 이 규칙을 관리하는 방식으로 오랫동안 iptables를 써왔는데, 이를 더 효율적인 후속 도구인 nftables로 바꾼 과정과 그 과정에서 배운 점을 공유하려고 해요. 1. kube-proxy latency가 서비스 안정성에 영향을 미쳤어요 쿠버네티스에서 노드가 새로 생기고 Pod가 뜨는 것은 매우 자연스러운 일이죠. 그런데 새 노드에 Pod가 스케줄링되고 애플리케이션이 시작되었다고 해서, 다른 서비스와 통신할 준비도 모두 끝난 걸까요? kube-proxy는 각 노드에서 Service로 향하는 트래픽이 실제 Pod에 도달할 수 있게 네트워크 규칙(이하 ‘규칙’)을 관리 하는데요, 새 노드에서는 이 규칙을 준비하는 동안 애플리케이션이 먼저 시작하면 DNS 조회나 다른 서비스와의 통신에 실패할 수 있어요. kube-proxy의 규칙 동기화가 느려지고 있다는 것은 예전부터 알고 있었어요. 2024년부터 지표를 지켜보니, 다른 리전보다 규모가 큰 한국 프로덕션에서 유독 지연이 높았거든요. 그러나 운영상 문제가 될 정도는 아니라고 판단했고, 실제로도 이슈로 이어진 적은 없었어요. 하지만 올해 상반기에 Karpenter를 도입하는 큰 변화가 있었어요. 노드를 빠르게 scale-out할 수 있게 되면서 Pod가 사용할 노드를 미리 준비하던 Overprovisioner를 더 이상 사용하지 않게 됐어요. 그 결과 새로 생성된 노드에 Pod가 곧바로 스케줄링되는 상황을 더 자주 마주했어요. 규칙 동기화가 끝나기 전에 애플리케이션이 통신을 시도할 가능성도 커진 거죠. 이후에 아래와 같은 문의가 들어오기 시작했고, 대부분은 ‘Pod가 통신이 안 된다’라는 제보였어요. 2024년과 2026년의 kube-proxy 지표를 나란히 놓고 보니, 2년 사이 kube-proxy의 부담이 크게 늘어난 걸 뚜렷하게 확인할 수 있었어요. 서비스 규모와 NAT 규칙 수가 눈에 띄게 늘었고, Pod가 생성되고 종료되는 일도 잦아졌어요. Pod가 바뀔 때마다 Service의 목적지를 나타내는 Endpoint, 즉 트래픽을 받을 Pod의 IP도 함께 바뀌기 때문에 kube-proxy가 반영해야 할 변경도 그만큼 늘어났어요. 그 결과 규칙 동기화 지연은 이전보다 몇 배 커졌고, 아직 규칙에 반영되지 못한 Endpoint 변경을 나타내는 endpoint changes pending 지표도 과거에는 잠깐씩 튀던 값이 지속적으로 쌓이는 모습으로 바뀌었어요. 2024년의 latency와 endpoint changes pending 2026년의 latency와 endpoint changes pending 2024년의 network programming rate 2026년의 network programming rate 2026년 상반기 당시 서비스 클러스터에는 약 1,400개의 Service와 27,000개의 Pod가 있었고, iptables의 NAT 규칙은 약 80,000개에 달했어요. 배포와 오토스케일링으로 Endpoint가 계속 바뀌는 가운데, 노드가 반복적으로 종료되고 생성될 때는 첫 규칙 동기화에 최대 4분 20초 가 걸리기도 했어요. 4분 넘게 Service와 DNS 통신이 안 되는 상태였던 거예요! 실제 서비스 운영에 영향을 주는 문제라는 것을 확인했기 때문에 이 문제를 해결해야 했어요. 팀원들과 개선 방안을 치열하게 의논한 결과 iptables 모드에서 nftables 모드로 전환해 보기로 했어요. 두 모드의 차이점은 다음과 같아요. iptables 모드에서 kube-proxy는 Service마다, 그리고 Endpoint마다 규칙을 만들어요. 패킷이 들어오면 먼저 Service 규칙을 위에서부터 차례로 비교해 목적지 Service를 찾고, 다시 그 Service의 Endpoint 규칙을 차례로 비교해 보낼 Pod를 골라요. 두 단계 모두 순차 비교라서 Service가 많을수록, 그리고 Service 하나에 붙은 Endpoint가 많을수록 비교할 규칙이 늘어나 조회 비용이 O(N)이에요. 더 큰 문제는 규칙을 갱신할 때예요. 전체 규칙 수는 Service와 Endpoint 수에 비례하고, 규칙이 많을수록 갱신 시간도 길어져요. 그런데 Endpoint는 Pod가 변경될 때 함께 바뀌어서 갱신이 자주 일어나다 보니, 반영하지 못한 변경이 점점 쌓였어요. 특히 kube-proxy가 시작한 직후에는 전체 규칙을 새로 쓰는 full sync를 하는데, 규모가 커진 당근 클러스터에서는 이 시간이 4분을 넘기도 했어요. nftables 모드는 Service를 찾는 단계와 Endpoint를 고르는 단계를 모두 map 기반으로 처리해요. 목적지 IP . 프로토콜 . 포트를 키로 map을 조회해서 해당 Service로 바로 이동하고, Endpoint도 목록을 하나씩 훑지 않고 map에서 바로 골라요. 그래서 Service나 Endpoint가 늘어나도 조회 비용은 O(1)에 가깝게 유지돼요. 갱신할 때도 지난 동기화 이후 바뀐 Service와 Endpoint만 반영하므로, 비용이 전체 규모가 아니라 변경량에 비례해요. Endpoint가 많고 자주 바뀌는 환경일수록 이 차이가 크게 드러나요. 하지만 모드를 변경하기 전에, 몇 가지 질문이 있었어요. 무엇이 규칙 동기화를 느리게 만들고 있었을까요? Service와 Endpoint가 많아서일까요? 변경이 자주 발생해서일까요? nftables로 바꾸면 얼마나 개선될까요? nftables 모드로 ‘안전하게’ 전환할 수 있을까요? 이 질문에 답하기 위해, 테스트 클러스터에서 조건을 바꿔가며 latency를 측정하고 iptables와 nftables를 비교하는 실험을 해보기로 했어요. 첫 동기화 시간을 20초 이내로 줄여야 한다고 판단했고, 실험으로 이를 검증하고자 했어요. 2. 실험의 네 가지 목표 실험을 시작하기 전에, 이 프로젝트에서 무엇을 확인할지 네 가지로 정리했어요. 1. 조건에 따른 규칙 동기화 지연 시간 확인 Service와 Endpoint가 많은 것과, 그 Endpoint가 자주 바뀌는 것은 다른 조건이겠죠? 같은 수의 Pod를 배포하더라도 조금씩 교체할 때와 한꺼번에 교체할 때의 영향이 다를 수 있고요. 규모, 변경 빈도, 배포 패턴을 나눠서 각각 latency에 어떤 영향을 주는지 측정해보기로 했어요. 2. 같은 조건에서 iptables와 nftables를 비교 nftables의 성능이 좋다고 알려져 있어도, 당근의 운영 환경에서 얼마나 개선될지는 직접 확인하고 싶었어요. 테스트 클러스터에서 같은 부하를 만들어 성능을 비교하기로 했어요. 3. 프로덕션에 안전하게 적용할 수 있는지 확인 테스트에서 빨라졌다고 바로 전환할 수는 없겠죠? 당근에서 사용하는 VPC CNI, Istio 등의 addon 구성과 충돌 없이 동작하는지, 알려진 이슈 중 우리 환경에 해당하는 것은 없는지 살펴봐야 했어요. 4. kube-proxy 버전을 유지할지, 함께 업그레이드할지 당시 EKS는 v1.34이지만, kube-proxy는 v1.34에서 이슈( https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135323 )가 발견되어 v1.31을 유지하고 있었어요. v1.31에서도 nftables 모드를 사용할 수 있었기 때문에, 모드만 변경하는 방법과 v1.34로 올리면서 변경하는 방법을 모두 검토했어요. 버전마다 성능과 알려진 이슈가 다를 수 있으니, 개선 폭과 운영 위험을 함께 비교해 결정하고자 했어요. 3. 먼저, 무엇을 측정

title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
abstract: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.

title: Put the World Back: Timestamps Matter in Time Series Reasoning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to time series reasoning. However, current evaluations often give models events in chronological order and already matched to the time series. This makes it unclear whether models use timestamps to connect events with observations or simply take shortcuts. To expose this ambiguity, we reformulate time series reasoning from a world-to-series projection perspective, viewing timestamps as explicit indices that connect numerical observations and external events to shared world states. We identify three structures that timestamps can make explicit: temporal causal structure, time semantics, and event-series alignment. Building on this perspective, we develop a diagnostic protocol that distinguishes timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts, a distinction that accuracy-based benchmarks cannot make. Controlled interventions on 310 questions from two tasks show that high accuracy can persist when timestamps are replaced by relative offsets or removed, while breaking event-series alignment induces systematic failures. When context is pre-aligned, models barely need timestamps. When order is missing, they use dates to recall world knowledge. Without dates, they rely on correlational shortcuts and rarely notice incorrect timestamps. These findings show that high accuracy on pre-aligned, ordered inputs does not establish that a model uses timestamps to synchronize observations with the world. We release our code, model outputs, and trajectory labels at https://github.com/tingrui-huang/timestamps-matter.

title: Routeability Before Routing: Routeability Audit Protocol (RAP) and RouteabilityBench for Audited LLM Model Selection
abstract: LLM routing aims to choose, for each prompt, which model in a portfolio is most likely to answer correctly. This only makes sense when the benchmark contains enough prompt-specific variation for different models to be best on different inputs. On coarse-scored LLM benchmarks, however, many models often tie for the best score, and the single best model may already leave little room for improvement. We therefore propose a routeability-first audit, instantiated as RAP and RouteabilityBench, a runnable claim-verification package. The audit is retrospective: it runs once the benchmark-portfolio score matrix exists and before router comparisons are interpreted as general evidence, rather than certifying a portfolio that has not yet been evaluated. Across four benchmarks and 66 LLMs, generic routing enhancements such as larger embedding sets, dimensionality reduction, selective abstention, clustering, and stronger regressors do not consistently outperform the single best model. The clearest positive evidence is concentrated in portfolio-dependent Omni-MATH settings, while GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval show different ways in which routing can remain hard or predictor-sensitive. Our practical recommendation is that routing gains should be reported together with routeability diagnostics, tied-best analysis, portfolio construction details, and family-corrected statistical tests.

title: Transferring Architecture as an Optimization Prior
abstract: Initialization determines the optimization "fate" of a model, going far beyond just setting the scale of its weights. It establishes a fundamental initial geometry over the input data, dictating certain aspects such as which examples are considered close and which representations gradient descent will naturally refine first. In this paper, we view the initial geometry of a network as an optimization prior and ask whether a network can change its optimization prior by referencing a completely different architecture. To investigate this question, we use an initialization procedure where a target network is aligned to the representational geometry of a randomly initialized guide network before any downstream training occurs. Crucially, alignment to the guide network cannot transfer learned features, never receives gradients, and does not use labels. We demonstrate that this cross-architecture transfer of "fate" benefits the target network in two key domains: (1) instilling the optimization benefits of depth into shallow networks by aligning them to deeper networks, and (2) transferring representational granularity by using fine-resolution networks to shape the geometry of networks with coarser representations. In both cases, the alignment results in improved downstream performance of the target network. Ultimately, this demonstrates that a model's architectural destiny can be decoupled from its physical structure and explicitly modified at initialization.

title: When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models
abstract: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift.
